title: Tree species mixing mitigates soil carbon loss by maintaining microbial necromass during forest conversion
content:
Our findings suggest that soil carbon losses during natural forest-to-plantation conversion are linked less to changes in lignin-derived plant carbon than to weakened microbial necromass formation and retention. Maintaining mixed stands, rather than replacing natural broadleaved forests with pure conifer plantations, may therefore provide a more effective strategy for sustaining microbial necromass-mediated SOC storage. Plantation management should incorporate microbial necromass indicators into soil carbon assessments and prioritize stand compositions that support fungal-dominated carbon stabilization pathways.

Abstract

Conversion of natural forests to plantations is a widespread land-use change with major consequences for soil organic carbon (SOC) storage. Forest management often aims to enhance carbon sequestration by increasing plant biomass and residue inputs, yet whether mixed stands can better maintain SOC by sustaining microbial-derived carbon remains unclear. We examined a forest conversion sequence from Mongolian oak (Quercus mongolica) natural forests to oak-Chinese pine (Pinus tabuliformis) mixed stands and pure Chinese pine plantations under different thinning intensities. Using biomarker-based approaches, we quantified SOC, microbial necromass carbon (MNC) and lignin phenols across two soil depths, and evaluated their relationships with soil physicochemical properties and microbial attributes. SOC declined along the conversion gradient from natural forests and mixed stands to pure plantations. Mixed stands retained higher MNC than pure plantations, particularly through fungal necromass pathways, whereas differences among pure plantations with different thinning intensities were limited. Variation in SOC was more closely associated with MNC than with lignin phenol content. Structural equation modelling further showed that MNC had a strong direct positive effect on SOC, while lignin phenols influenced SOC mainly through indirect pathways. Synthesis and applications. Our findings suggest that soil carbon losses during natural forest-to-plantation conversion are linked less to changes in lignin-derived plant carbon than to weakened microbial necromass formation and retention. Maintaining mixed stands, rather than replacing natural broadleaved forests with pure conifer plantations, may therefore provide a more effective strategy for sustaining microbial necromass-mediated SOC storage. Plantation management should incorporate microbial necromass indicators into soil carbon assessments and prioritize stand compositions that support fungal-dominated carbon stabilization pathways.
